opus-5.5.text:
Well, when Peter Norvig and I started writing the textbook in the early nineties, the field was quite fragmented. You had people working on logical reasoning, on probabilistic inference, on planning, on computer vision, on natural language, on robotics, and on machine learning. They went to different conferences, used different notation, and often didn't think they had much to say to each other. Some even thought of themselves as working on entirely different problems.

What struck us was that all of these pieces are really in service of one thing: building systems that act well. An agent perceives its environment and chooses actions, and the question is what it should do given what it has perceived so far and what it is trying to achieve. Once you frame it that way, each subfield finds its natural place. Perception is how the agent gets information about the world. Knowledge representation and reasoning are how it maintains and uses what it knows. Probabilistic methods handle the fact that it's uncertain. Planning and decision theory are how it chooses actions that lead to good outcomes. And learning is how it improves all of those components from experience.

So the agent framework isn't just an organizing device for chapters in a book. It gives you a common standard of success, which is rational behavior, and it tells you how the components have to fit together. It also forces you to ask questions you might otherwise ignore. For example, what is the performance measure? Is the environment fully or partially observable? Is it deterministic or stochastic? Are there other agents? Those properties determine which techniques are appropriate. A lot of confusion in AI comes from people using a method designed for one kind of environment in another.

It also connects AI to economics, control theory, operations research and statistics, which have been studying optimal decision-making for a long time. That's a healthy thing. AI isn't a bag of tricks, it's the study of how to make good decisions computationally.

I should add a caveat, which has become central to my thinking over the last decade. The standard version of the framework assumes that we give the machine a fixed objective, and it optimizes it. That turns out to be a mistake once systems become very capable, because we can't specify objectives completely and correctly. If the objective is wrong, a more capable optimizer just does more damage. So I've argued that we need to revise the framework: the machine should be pursuing our objectives, but it should be explicitly uncertain about what those are, and it should learn about them from our behavior. That keeps the agent perspective, which I still think is the right foundation, but changes the relationship between the machine and the humans it's supposed to benefit.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, when Peter Norvig and I sat down to write the textbook, we faced a field that looked less like a discipline and more like a collection of tribes. You had the logic people, the probability people, the neural network people, the planning people, the robotics people, and they often didn't talk to each other, and in some cases actively disparaged each other's work. So the question was, what is the thing that all of these people are actually trying to do?

And the answer, it seemed to us, was that they're all trying to build systems that perceive something about their environment and then act on it. An agent, in the simplest sense, is just something that maps percept sequences to actions. Once you adopt that view, the various subfields stop looking like competitors and start looking like components. Logic is a way of representing what the agent knows. Probability handles the fact that the agent is uncertain. Search and planning are about choosing actions that achieve goals. Learning is how the agent improves its mapping over time from experience. Perception and natural language are how the information gets in. And so on.

The other thing the agent view gives you is a notion of what it means to do well. We borrowed the idea of rationality from economics and decision theory: an agent is rational if it acts to maximize its expected utility given what it knows. That gives you a standard against which to measure any approach, whether it's a hand-coded expert system or a deep reinforcement learning policy. It also makes clear that intelligence is not about one particular technique. The technique that matters is whatever gets you closer to that standard in a given environment with given computational resources.

Now, I'd add that I've become more cautious about one part of that story over the years. The framework assumes the objective is given, fixed, and correct. In the textbook we took that for granted, and most of the field still does. But if you build a very capable agent and hand it a slightly wrong objective, the rational thing for it to do is pursue that wrong objective extremely effectively. So the agent framework remains, I think, the right unifying lens, but the next step is to be honest that the objective itself is uncertain, that the machine should know it doesn't fully know what we want, and that it should treat learning our preferences as part of the problem rather than a precondition for it.

astra-6.text:
Well, the agent framework gives us a common question: how should a system act, given what it has perceived? An agent receives information from its environment and acts on that environment. Once you start there, the different areas of AI become parts of a larger problem rather than separate intellectual enterprises.

Perception tells you something about the state of the world. Learning allows you to improve your understanding from experience. Reasoning helps you work out the consequences of what you know, and planning helps you choose actions. Language is another way of obtaining information and affecting the world, through communication with other agents.

The point isn’t that every system has to contain every one of those capabilities. It’s that we can understand what each capability is for, and how to evaluate it, by asking how it contributes to the agent’s behavior. You might have a beautiful theorem prover, for example, but an agent also has to decide which questions are worth proving things about, and how much time to spend before acting.

So it provides a unifying perspective without prescribing a single architecture. A very simple reactive system and a system that deliberates extensively can both be understood as agents. What matters is whether their behavior makes sense given the information and resources available to them.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the agent framework gives us a way to talk about what all these different capabilities are for. An agent perceives its environment and acts on it, and the question is how those actions can produce good outcomes. Vision, language, reasoning, learning, planning—all of those contribute to that process.

If you study them in isolation, it’s easy to lose sight of the purpose. You might ask whether a vision system correctly labels an image. But for an agent, the more fundamental question is whether it extracts the information needed to decide what to do. And sometimes that means taking an action to get more information—looking somewhere else, asking a question, running an experiment. So perception and action are connected, as are learning and decision-making.

The framework doesn’t require that everything use the same technique. It gives the different techniques a common setting and a common question: how does this contribute to intelligent behavior? Then, of course, we have to be very careful about what we mean by a good outcome, and whose preferences determine that.
